source.title: Universal Boosts, Specific Suppressors: Sparse Autoencoder Steering of Medical Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Farhad Nooralahzadeh; Benjamin Gundersen; Nicolas Deperrois; Hidetoshi Matsuom; Mizuho Nishio; Thomas Frauenfelder; Ahmed Allam; Christian Blüthgen; Michael Moor; Michael Krauthammer

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests cross-model similarity in SAE-feature functions using causal error-type profiles and similarity measures, rather than comparing representations with the original claim’s distance-based approach.
record.gate_note: The cross-model functional-overlap analysis in Table 4 measures how similarly SAE features affect clinical error types across model pairs; these results bear on V5. The steering quality gains and error counts are not rows because they do not measure representational convergence or recurring features. The paper states that SAE indices are not directly comparable across architectures, so the overlap analysis compares functional profiles, not feature identity.
record.test_reason: The cross-model analysis (Table 4, App. E) does not ask whether the same features recur across models. It compares 4-dimensional summaries of each model's top-100 steering features: the mean causal-effect vector over four GREEN error types (FF/MF/WL/WS), and the distribution of which error type each feature affects most. High similarity means the feature sets push the same error types in similar proportions. It does not show that matching interpretable features, neurons or circuits exist across models. The authors say SAE indices are not comparable across architectures, so no feature-to-feature matching is attempted. This is a related but different construct, so it goes under fits_no_version. The rest of the paper is SAE steering performance, which is not on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that boost features have similar functional (error-type) profiles across the three medical VLMs, while suppress features are model-specific. They read this as boost priors being transferable and suppress lists needing re-derivation per backbone. They explain the gap by boost features encoding general radiology-writing habits and suppress features encoding model-specific template traps. Their IU-Xray claim that features are 'properties of the model' concerns transfer across datasets within RadVLM, not convergence across models.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares causal error-type profiles of separately trained SAE features across medical VLM architectures, using weighted Jaccard and cosine similarity; it does not measure representation distances between matched inputs or test convergence with model scale.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity depends on feature direction: boost profiles are consistently more similar than suppress profiles across all model pairs. The study reports both weighted Jaccard and cosine measures, with the same qualitative boost–suppress pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: Across three medical VLMs (RadVLM/Qwen3-VL-8B, LLaVA-Rad 7B, CheXOne/Qwen2.5-VL-3B), the error-type profiles of quality-promoting (boost) SAE steering features are similar. Weighted Jaccard is 0.65–0.75 and signature cosine 0.91–0.95. Hallucination-linked (suppress) profiles are less similar: Jaccard 0.41–0.58, cosine 0.25–0.52. Aggregates are over layers 8/16/20/24 and no null baseline is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The causal error-type profiles of SAE steering features (functional roles at a coarse task level) are more similar across independently trained models for quality-promoting directions than for error-promoting directions.

record.code_released: https://cxr-sparse-feature-dashboard.netlify.app/ (interactive feature dashboard; code release not stated)
record.problems: Only three medical radiology VLMs and four steered layers are compared. Bootstrap intervals are based on the four layer values. The overlap measure compares functional error-type profiles rather than shared feature identities or representation geometry. The paper notes that interactions between SAE dictionary size, sparsity, and model scale are not fully characterized.
record.rows_left_out: None of the cross-model overlap results in Table 4 were left out. Main steering outcomes and clinical error-count results in Table 1, Table 2, and Appendix F were excluded because they do not measure the claim’s representational convergence.

untested.parts: No scale sweep and no representational similarity between models.
No image-caption alignment between vision and language models.
No mapping, stitching or transfer of representations between models; each model gets its own SAE.
No matching of individual SAE features, neurons or circuits across models; only aggregate error-type profiles of steering-feature sets are compared.
No test of how a convergence measure depends on metric, settings or inputs.
No test of how far alignment goes or what causes it.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests V5' was overturned: two 4-dimensional summaries of feature sets cannot show that the same features recur, and there is no chance baseline. The text's gloss that 65–75% of boost features overlap is wrong: Ruzicka here is computed on categorical error-type distributions, not feature sets. CIs come from bootstrapping only four layer values. None of the original sources is cited.

versions.untested_parts: No scale sweep or measurement of representational distances between independently trained models.
No paired image-caption representation alignment or comparison of vision and language model capability.
No comparison across random initializations of the same architecture.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test.
The study compares SAE features’ functional error-type profiles, not whether identical interpretable features, neurons, or circuits recur across models.
The study does not test convergence of input-distance geometry across measures, settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
No test of whether shared training data or objectives explain cross-model representational alignment, or whether alignment plateaus.

rows.subject: RadVLM vs. LLaVA-Rad
rows.stage_stated: RadVLM: radiology instruction-tuned; LLaVA-Rad: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared cross-model profiles of top-100 SAE features by error-type causal effects; similarity aggregated over layers 8, 16, 20, and 24.
rows.measure: Weighted Jaccard similarity of feature error-type profiles
rows.note: Compares functional error-type profiles, not shared SAE indices or feature identity.
rows.check: Ruzicka similarity of 4-category dominant-error-type distributions for the boost sets, not recurrence of features. No chance or null baseline is given; with only 4 categories and boost sets dominated by FF (e.g. 494/500 at l=24 for RadVLM), high overlap could arise without shared features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Boost-feature functional profiles across the three model pairs
reader_labels.reason: Boost profiles show higher cross-model similarity, with weighted Jaccard 0.65–0.75 and cosine 0.91–0.95 (R1–R6). This supports shared functional roles, but does not establish recurrence of identical features.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Suppress-feature functional profiles across the three model pairs
reader_labels.reason: Suppress profiles are less similar than boost profiles across all pairs; the LLaVA-Rad–CheXOne cosine is 0.25 [0.12, 0.40] (R7–R12). The comparison concerns feature functions, not recurrence of the same features.
